progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From bio-m5-b01: sexual reproduction mixes alleles from two parents; asexual reproduction copies one parent; varied offspring and identical offspring. From bio-m5-b06a: DNA in prokaryotes and eukaryotes; bacteria carry plasmids. From B6b and B6c (Module 5): a gene codes for a protein; cells read genes to make proteins. From b01 and b08 (Module 6): alleles, the gene pool, allele frequency; gene flow and selection change how common alleles are. From Year 11: selective pressure and natural selection. Not assumed: biotechnology as a defined field, fermentation as a process, selective breeding by name (it may be familiar), recombinant DNA, reproductive technologies, the four-way "what does it change" frame.
progression.startsWith: Compare yeast use and selective breeding with a modern technique. The video opens: A loaf of bread, a merino's fine wool, and a vial of human insulin.
progression.stopsAfter: defining biotechnology as deliberately using living organisms, cells or biological processes to make a product or solve a problem, in agriculture, medicine and industry; explaining that fermentation uses yeast's process (carbon dioxide raises bread) with the yeast's DNA unchanged; explaining that selective breeding chooses parents, so it changes which existing alleles are passed on and how common they become, but changes no organism's DNA; explaining that insulin moved from animal pancreases (from 1922) to bacteria carrying DNA coding for human insulin (from 1982), a change to the bacteria's DNA, called recombinant DNA; sorting current technologies by what they change (a process used; the parents chosen, as in artificial insemination and pollination; DNA copied, as in cloning; DNA inserted or edited, as in insulin bacteria, Bt cotton and gene editing) and stating each kind's advantage; explaining that old methods are still used alongside new ones; applying this to an unseen classification item and an unseen compare item.
progression.nextLesson: how plant and animal biotechnology should be judged (route entry bio-m6-b10).

teaching.task: Bread, fine wool and human insulin all come from biotechnology, but only one needed DNA changed in a lab. So what counts as biotechnology, and what does each kind actually change?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why bread rises (yeast releases CO₂ that is trapped as bubbles, 2); why fermentation counts as biotechnology though no DNA changes (the definition is about using living processes, 3); why selective breeding changes a flock without changing any sheep's DNA (choosing parents changes which alleles are passed on, 4); why it is slow and limited (existing alleles only, generations, 4, 7); why insulin bacteria are different (DNA coding for human insulin was put into them, and they read it like their own genes, 5); why each kind has its advantage (what it changes decides what it can do, 7); why old methods persist (they still work, especially for many-gene traits, 8). Visible case: three products, one board; each lane shows what happens to the DNA. Video advantage: CO₂ bubbles drifting into the crumb, rings reshuffling into an offspring strip, a strip duplicating, an amber segment sliding into a plasmid. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; the attempt 1 card is the densest frame and is the task itself.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Bread, fine merino wool and human insulin all come from biotechnology, but only one needed DNA changed in a lab, so the question is what counts as biotechnology and what each kind actually changes; yeast shows a process used with its DNA unchanged, the definition follows, selective breeding shows parents chosen so alleles are passed on and become more common with no DNA changed, and insulin from bacteria shows DNA inserted (recombinant DNA named); the four-lane board then sorts every case by what is changed (a process used, the parents chosen, DNA copied, DNA inserted or edited), adds the advantage of each, and a timeline shows old methods still in use beside new ones. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: A loaf of bread, a merino's fine wool, and a vial of human insulin. All three come from biotechnology. But only one of them needed anyone to change an organism's DNA in a lab, and people were baking with yeast thousands of years before anyone knew DNA existed. So what counts as biotechnology, and what does each kind actually change?
teaching.understandingCheck: 10a is an identify item: four examples (yoghurt made with bacteria; semen from one bull used to inseminate many cows; banana plants grown from suckers of one parent; cotton carrying a gene from a soil bacterium); identify what each changes, and state which change an organism's DNA sequence. It tests the four-way frame and the route stop. 10c is a compare item: selective breeding against recombinant DNA technology as ways to get caterpillar-resistant cotton. It tests the compare verb on the same criteria (what changes, source of the trait, time). Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the full card stays on screen during and after the countdown. Each feedback is brief (about 20 to 30 s): answer, key reason, the givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B6-IQ2-01: "investigate the uses and applications of biotechnology (past, present and future), including: (ACSBL087)". B6-IQ3-01 (absorbed from b14): "investigate the uses and advantages of current genetic technologies that induce genetic change". The B6-IQ2-01 sub-points ("analysing the social implications and ethical uses ...", "researching future directions ...", "evaluating the potential benefits ...", "evaluating the changes to the Earth's biodiversity ...") belong to b10 to b13 and are not claimed here. This video owns first coverage of the B6-IQ2-01 stem (uses and applications, past and present) and the framing half of B6-IQ3-01 (what each current technology changes and its advantage); b15 to b18 complete B6-IQ3-01 technique by technique. Update the ledger rows when this design passes review. The verbs are carried by the attempts: "identify" (attempt 1, a classification with a reason) and "compare" (attempt 2, the same criteria on both sides; what-markers-reward: "deal with the same feature on both sides").

design.visualSystem: One "What does it change?" board built across the video: four lanes, each with a painted object above and a coded DNA strip below (b01's `SlimStrand`, slim, cream bands, never coloured bars on a painted cell). Lane 1 "uses a process": yeast plate and bread plate; the strip stays unchanged (a small tick). Lane 2 "chooses the parents": merino plate, then the insemination straw and tank plate and the paintbrush pollination plate; below, two parental strips with b01 `AlleleRing` markers, and an offspring strip receiving one ring from each (reshuffled, no new ring), plus a small flock `FillBar` that rises over generations. Lane 3 "copies DNA": tissue-culture jars plate and a strawberry runner plate; the strip duplicates into identical copies. Lane 4 "inserts or edits DNA": bacterium-with-plasmid plate, insulin vial, Bt cotton plate; the strip gains an amber inserted segment. The lanes appear one per scene (2, 4, 6, 6) and are complete by scene 6; scene 7 adds one advantage chip under each lane. A coded timeline (scene 8) runs left to right, "thousands of years ago", "1922", "1982", "today", with sector icons (agriculture, medicine, industry) as small coded glyphs. Real objects are painted plates; DNA, allele rings, bars and the timeline are coded. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items on screen at once besides small grey lane labels; each tag fades when the next cue lands; completed lanes dim to grey thumbnails while a new lane is active.
design.transitionPlan: The three product plates open the hook; the "What does it change?" board builds one lane per scene, each painted object above its coded DNA strip (unchanged with a tick, reshuffled allele rings with a rising flock bar, identical copies, an amber inserted segment); scene 7 adds one advantage chip under each lane; the timeline draws left to right with sector icons while the board shrinks; the memory aid writes large; each attempt clears the board and its feedback underlines the question as the lanes return small; the decision rule chips and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.
